title: Generations and politics in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about age, trust and the rise of parties that promise to take on 'the system', from Britain, Germany and across Europe.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Age is now one of politics' sharpest lines.
paras: In several of these, the gap between young and old was wider than the room expected, and in others, the share backing parties outside the mainstream was larger.
What those numbers mean, and what a democracy owes to the people on each side of them, is the argument worth having.

questions.q: A 2026 study of 31 European countries counted voters for authoritarian and populist parties. Roughly what share of European voters now back one?
questions.explain: About one in three European voters now back an authoritarian or populist party across the 31 countries, a historic high. In the 1950s and 1960s it was about one in ten, and by 2019 it was just under 30%.
questions.source: Timbro, Authoritarian Populism Index, October 2026 (reported by EUobserver, 26 October 2026)

questions.q: What share of the vote did the AfD win in Germany's federal election in February 2025?
questions.explain: The AfD won 20.8%, about double its 10.4% in 2021, and came second. It was the party's best result in a federal election.

questions.q: In the same election, which party won the most votes among 18- to 24-year-olds?
questions.explain: Die Linke won about 26% of 18- to 24-year-olds, with the AfD second on about 21% and the CDU/CSU on 13%. Young voters moved away from the centre in both directions, and young women and young men often in opposite ones.
questions.source: Forschungsgruppe Wahlen, reported by ZDFheute, 24 February 2025

questions.q: Half of Scotland's population is older than what age (mid-2025)?
questions.explain: Scotland's median age is 43.1, well above England's 40.6. In every UK nation the number of people aged 65 and over rose in the year to mid-2025, while the number aged 15 and under fell.
questions.source: ONS, Population estimates for the UK, England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland: mid-2025 (October 2026)

questions.q: In the 2024 UK general election, what share of voters under 30 voted Conservative?
questions.explain: Only 8% of under-30s voted Conservative, against 46% of voters aged 70 and over. Age has become one of the sharpest dividing lines in how people in Britain vote.
questions.source: YouGov, How Britain voted in the 2024 general election

questions.q: Ipsos has asked Britons since 1983 which professions they trust to tell the truth. What share trusted politicians in 2025?
questions.sub: trust politicians to tell the truth
questions.explain: Just 9% trusted politicians to tell the truth, joint lowest since the survey began in 1983; government ministers scored 14%. Only social media influencers, at 6%, did worse.

questions.q: A 2025 survey in 28 countries asked whether hostile actions, such as attacking people online, spreading false information or violence, are acceptable to bring about change. What share of 18- to 34-year-olds approved of at least one?
questions.explain: More than half of 18- to 34-year-olds (53%) approved of at least one form of 'hostile activism', against 40% of all respondents. Six in ten people said they felt a moderate or high sense of grievance.

questions.q: In 2023, what share of UK 12- to 15-year-olds used TikTok as a source of news?
questions.sub: of 12- to 15-year-olds, their top single news source
questions.explain: 28% of 12- to 15-year-olds got news from TikTok, up 17 points since 2020, making it their most-used single news source, just ahead of YouTube and Instagram (25% each). Among 16- to 24-year-olds, 71% got news from social media, against 47% of all adults.
questions.source: Ofcom, News Consumption in the UK 2023
